FRD-001.q: Match the three ACFE Fraud Tree categories with examples:
FRD-001.e: Per ACFE reports, asset misappropriation is most common while financial statement fraud has the largest median loss.
p: An employee creates a ghost vendor to withdraw cash
The procurement head takes supplier kickbacks
Booking fictitious year-end revenue to hit targets
FRD-001.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Tree (Occupational Fraud and Abuse Classification System); ACFE Report to the Nations 2024.
Analysis: Asset misappropriation – stealing or misusing assets (ghost vendors draining cash). Corruption – misusing influence in dealings for gain (kickbacks, conflicts of interest, bribery). Financial statement fraud – intentional misstatement (fake revenue to hit targets).
Note: In ACFE's 2024 report, asset misappropriation is about 89% of cases with the lowest median loss; FS fraud about 5% of cases with the highest median loss (around USD 766k). Figures vary by edition.

FRD-002.q: Match each fraud triangle (Cressey) element with an example:
p: Large personal debts, unrealistic bonus targets
One person approves and pays, no one checks
'I'm only borrowing; the company owes me more'
FRD-002.x:
Basis: Donald Cressey (1953) – fraud triangle; VSA 240 appendix 1.
Analysis: Pressure/incentive – financial need or strain (personal debt, excessive bonus targets). Opportunity – conditions allowing commission and concealment (one person approving and paying, no checks). Rationalisation – how the perpetrator justifies it ('just borrowing', 'the company owes me').
Note: Entities most directly control 'opportunity' through IC design; pressure and rationalisation are influenced only indirectly (culture, bonus policy).

FRD-003.q: Which element does the Fraud Diamond add to the fraud triangle?
FRD-003.e: Senior, system-savvy, confident people able to coerce others can commit large frauds.
o: Capability – position, knowledge, ability to manipulate and conceal
FRD-003.x:
Basis: Wolfe & Hermanson (2004), 'The Fraud Diamond', CPA Journal.
Analysis: The fraud diamond adds a fourth element – capability: a position or function allowing one to create or exploit opportunity; intelligence and knowledge of systems and control gaps; confidence, ability to coerce others, lie consistently and handle stress. Someone with opportunity but no capability rarely commits large, sustained fraud.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't elements of the model.

FRD-004.q: Per recent ACFE reports, tips are the most common detection method, and employees are the largest tip source.
FRD-004.e: True. An effective whistleblowing channel is therefore a key detective control.
FRD-004.x:
Basis: ACFE – Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations.
Analysis: True. Tips are the most common detection method (about 43% of cases in 2024), far ahead of internal audit and management review; employees are the largest source (around half), followed by customers and vendors. Entities with hotlines detect fraud faster with smaller losses → an effective channel (ICA-079) is a key detective control.
Note: Exact percentages vary by edition.

FRD-005.q: The fundamental difference between fraud and error under VSA 240 is:
FRD-005.e: Fraud is an intentional act to obtain an unjust or illegal advantage.
FRD-005.x:
Basis: VSA 240 paras 2–3, 11.
Analysis: The distinguishing factor is intent: fraud is an intentional act by one or more members of governance, management, staff or third parties, using deception to gain an unjust or illegal advantage; error is unintentional.
Distractors: B – amount doesn't define the nature; C – anyone can commit either; D – detection timing is irrelevant.

FRD-006.q: Select ALL common behavioural red flags of fraud perpetrators:
FRD-006.e: Per ACFE, living beyond means and financial difficulties are the most common.
o: Unusually close ties with a vendor/customer
Refusing leave or to share duties
FRD-006.x:
Basis: ACFE Report to the Nations 2024 (behavioural red flags).
Analysis: Common behavioural red flags: (A) living beyond means – the most common (about 39% of perpetrators); (B) personal financial difficulties; (C) unusually close ties with vendors or customers; (D) refusing leave, controlling work tightly, shutting others out – to sustain concealment (ICA-065, FRD-068). Most perpetrators show at least one.
Distractors: (E) Proposing transparent process improvements is positive behaviour.

FRD-007.q: Fraud by senior managers usually causes larger losses than by junior staff because:
FRD-007.e: Seniority and authority increase both opportunity and concealment capability.
o: They can override controls, access large assets and conceal or collude
FRD-007.x:
Basis: ACFE Report to the Nations (losses by position); VSA 240 para 31.
Analysis: Owners/executives cause median losses many times those of employees because they can override controls; access large assets and transactions; conceal (directing subordinates, adjusting records) and collude; face less oversight; and their schemes run longer.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main reasons.

FRD-008.q: Collusion among several people can defeat segregation of duties.
FRD-008.e: True. It's an inherent limitation; detective controls like analytics, rotation and hotlines are needed.
FRD-008.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (inherent limitations); ACFE.
Analysis: True. Segregation assumes one person checks another; when two or more collude (preparer and approver, storekeeper and guard), the control fails (ICA-089). ACFE finds multi-perpetrator schemes cause markedly larger losses. Compensate with detective controls: data analytics, job rotation, mandatory leave, hotlines, surprise checks.

FRD-009.q: Primary responsibility for preventing and detecting fraud rests with:
FRD-009.e: The auditor is responsible for reasonable assurance that the FS are free of material misstatement due to fraud or error.
o: Those charged with governance and management
FRD-009.x:
Basis: VSA 240 paras 4–5.
Analysis: Primary responsibility for preventing and detecting fraud rests with governance and management: an honest culture, IC and oversight. The auditor is responsible for obtaining reasonable assurance that the FS are free from material misstatement, whether from fraud or error – not for finding all fraud (FRD-080).
Distractors: B misplaces the role; C – tax authorities administer tax; D – IA supports but isn't the sole party; ultimate responsibility remains with governance and management.

FRD-010.q: The two fraud types relevant to an FS audit under VSA 240 are:
FRD-010.e: Corruption usually shows through one of these when it affects the FS.
o: Fraudulent financial reporting and misappropriation of assets
FRD-010.x:
Basis: VSA 240 para 3, A1–A6.
Analysis: Two kinds of intentional misstatement matter to FS audits: fraudulent financial reporting (deliberate misstatements or omissions of amounts or disclosures to deceive users) and misappropriation of assets (theft of entity assets, often with false records to hide it). Corruption affecting the FS usually appears as one of these.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't VSA 240 categories.

FRD-011.e: Signs: delayed postings, customer balance disputes, staff refusing leave.
o: Stealing customer A's payment, then using customer B's to credit A, continuously concealing
FRD-011.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual (skimming – lapping).
Analysis: Lapping: an employee takes customer A's payment, then applies customer B's payment to A's account, then C's to B's… – a chain of concealment that must be kept going, with the shortfall growing. Red flags: credits posted later than receipt, customer balance complaints, remittance names not matching, employees not taking leave.
Distractors: B is plain skimming; C is FS fraud; D – voiding invoices is a different scheme.

FRD-012.e: Balance adjustment rights must be separate from collectors.
o: Separate cash receipt from AR posting
Customers pay by bank into the company account with automated matching
Independent staff send periodic statements directly to customers
FRD-012.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10; ACFE.
Analysis: Anti-lapping controls: (A) separate cash receipt from receivables posting – no one can both take cash and credit accounts at will; (B) customers pay by bank into company accounts with automatic matching – removing cash from staff hands; (C) independent staff send statements to customers – who spot wrong balances; (D) mandatory leave and rotation – breaking the concealment chain.
Distractors: (E) Letting the cashier adjust receivables is precisely the concealment opportunity.

FRD-013.q: Which is the strongest sign of a ghost (shell) vendor?
FRD-013.e: Matching the vendor master against HR data is an effective analytic test.
o: A new vendor whose address/bank account matches an employee's, only service invoices, no goods received
A supplier on a multi-year framework contract
FRD-013.x:
Basis: ACFE – billing schemes, shell companies.
Analysis: Ghost-vendor signs: newly created; address, phone or bank account matching an employee's; only service invoices (hard to verify) and no goods received; a mailbox or home address; no tax code or a freshly registered one. An effective test: match the vendor master to HR data (FRD-029).
Distractors: B, C and D describe legitimate vendors with history and real deliveries.

FRD-014.q: The CFO's approval threshold is above VND 100 million. Analysis shows one employee raised 18 payment requests of 98–99.9 million to the same vendor, totalling 1,770 million. What is the average request (VND million)?
FRD-014.e: 1,770/18 ≈ 98.33 million – a sign of split purchases to avoid approval thresholds.
FRD-014.x:
Basis: ACFE – split purchases to evade approval limits.
Working: Average = 1,770 / 18 ≈ VND 98.33 million per request.
Analysis: 18 requests to one vendor by one preparer, all just under the 100 million limit → a sign of splitting to avoid CFO approval; the 1,770 million total should have gone to higher approval and perhaps tender. Test: filter items at 90–99.99% of the limit by preparer, vendor and period.
Check: 98.33 × 18 ≈ 1,770 ✓.

FRD-015.e: Check vendor ownership, benchmark prices, compare with buying direct from manufacturers.
o: An employee's intermediary company buys from the real supplier and resells to the employer at a markup
FRD-015.x:
Basis: ACFE – billing schemes (pass-through).
Analysis: Pass-through: an employee (usually in purchasing) sets up or secretly owns an intermediary that buys real goods from a real supplier and resells them to the company at a markup → goods are genuinely received, so it's hard to spot, and the markup goes to the employee. Detection: check vendors' beneficial ownership, compare prices with the market and with buying direct from manufacturers.
Distractors: B, C and D are other schemes.

FRD-016.q: Select ALL payroll fraud red flags:
FRD-016.e: On-time bank payment is not a red flag.
o: Employees without social insurance or tax IDs
Several employees paid into the same bank account
Overtime spikes in one unit approved by one supervisor
Wages paid by bank on time
FRD-016.x:
Basis: ACFE – payroll schemes (ghost employees, falsified hours).
Analysis: Payroll red flags: (A) staff without social insurance or tax codes – possibly non-existent; (B) several employees paid into one bank account – money going to one person; (C) leavers still on the payroll; (D) overtime spiking in one unit approved by one supervisor – padded hours.
Distractors: (E) Timely bank payment of wages is good practice.

FRD-017.q: At a supermarket chain, one store's shrinkage is 3x the chain average, concentrated in small high-value items. A sensible first investigative step:
FRD-017.e: Investigations need evidence before attributing individual responsibility.
o: Analyse data by shift/staff: voids, receipt-less returns, stock adjustments; review CCTV; surprise counts
FRD-017.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual (inventory shrinkage investigations).
Analysis: Shrinkage at 3× the average, concentrated in small high-value items (easy to carry out) → suspected internal theft. First: analyse data by shift and employee (voids, returns without receipts, stock adjustments), match to CCTV, and run surprise counts – gathering evidence before assigning blame.
Distractors: B concludes without evidence, a legal risk; C doesn't address the cause; D – 3× shrinkage isn't normal.

FRD-018.q: 'Skimming' takes cash before it is recorded, so it's harder to detect than 'larceny' (taking cash after recording).
FRD-018.e: True. Skimming leaves no trace in the books; independent operational data (POS, CCTV, goods issued) must be reconciled.
FRD-018.x:
Basis: ACFE – cash receipt schemes (skimming vs larceny).
Analysis: True. Skimming takes cash before it's recorded (unrecorded sales, cash taken without invoicing) → no trace in the books, balances still agree. Larceny takes cash after recording → a gap between books and cash, easier to catch via reconciliation. Detecting skimming needs independent operational data: POS, CCTV, goods issued, margin analysis by outlet.

FRD-019.q: An AP clerk changes a real vendor's bank account to a personal one and reverts it after payment. The most effective detective control:
FRD-019.e: Change-then-revert patterns are a classic sign.
o: Vendor master-data change logs reviewed independently, especially short-lived temporary changes
FRD-019.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P10–11 (master data controls).
Analysis: Temporarily changing the payee account and reverting it: the payables ledger still agrees, and the real supplier chases payment later. Best detective control: a vendor master change log reviewed by someone independent, focusing on change-and-revert within short windows and changes just before payment runs. Preventive: separate master data editing from payment creation, verify via independent channels (ICA-046).
Distractors: B – signatures are still valid; C – year-end is too late; D is irrelevant.

FRD-020.q: The most common expense reimbursement frauds are:
FRD-020.e: Controls: clear policy, original receipts, corporate cards, duplicate and exception analytics.
o: Claiming personal costs as business, fake receipts, inflated amounts, duplicate claims
FRD-020.x:
Basis: ACFE – expense reimbursement schemes.
Analysis: Four common forms: mischaracterised expenses (personal costs claimed as business); fictitious expenses (fake or non-existent receipts); overstated expenses (altered or inflated receipts); multiple reimbursements (one cost claimed several times). Controls: clear policy, original receipts, corporate cards, approval by someone who knows the work, analysis for duplicates and exceptions (weekends, holidays, round amounts).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't reimbursement schemes.

FRD-021.q: A fleet of 40 trucks has a standard of 30 litres/100 km. Last month GPS distance totalled 120,000 km and 43,200 litres were paid. How many litres exceed the standard?
FRD-021.e: Standard = 120,000 × 30/100 = 36,000 litres; excess 43,200 − 36,000 = 7,200 litres (20%) → investigate by vehicle/driver.
FRD-021.x:
Basis: ACFE (fuel fraud); COSO 2013 P13 (ICA-091).
Working: Standard = 120,000 × 30 / 100 = 36,000 litres; excess = 43,200 − 36,000 = 7,200 litres (7,200 / 36,000 = 20%).
Analysis: 20% over standard is significant → analyse by vehicle, driver, station and time to pinpoint (fuelling outside vehicles, resale, card misuse), ruling out legitimate causes (old trucks, mountain routes, outdated standards).
Check: 36,000 × 1.2 = 43,200 ✓.

FRD-022.q: Writing off inventory as 'scrapped' or 'damaged' without an independent committee and minutes is a way to conceal inventory theft.
FRD-022.e: True. The goods are actually sold outside.
FRD-022.x:
Basis: ACFE – concealing inventory theft; COSO 2013 P10 (ICA-082).
Analysis: True. Recording 'destroyed', 'damaged' or shrinkage without an independent committee, minutes or photo/video evidence → good stock is written off in the books but actually sold outside. It is a way to adjust stock records to hide shortages (write-off concealment). Controls: an independent destruction committee, witnessed disposal, analysis of write-off rates by warehouse and requester.

FRD-023.q: Which sign suggests bid rigging in procurement?
FRD-023.e: Analysing bid history helps reveal collusion patterns.
o: Bidders win in rotation, bids are close to each other and to the budget, losers become subcontractors
FRD-023.x:
Basis: ACFE – bid rigging; Law on Bidding 2023 (prohibited acts – collusion).
Analysis: Collusion signs: bidders winning in rotation (sharing the market); bids close to each other and to the package budget (no real competition); losers becoming subcontractors of the winner (sharing gains); bids with identical errors or submitted from the same IP address.
Distractors: B, C and D – many new bidders, winning prices well below budget and wide public invitations indicate competition.

FRD-024.q: Select ALL red flags of procurement kickbacks:
o: Persistently above-market prices from one vendor
Overlooking that vendor's poor quality and short deliveries
Selecting vendors via a transparent tender
FRD-024.x:
Basis: ACFE – corruption (kickback schemes).
Analysis: Kickback signs: (A) persistently above-market prices from one vendor – the excess funds the kickback; (B) overlooking poor quality and short deliveries – protecting the vendor; (C) resisting vendor changes or re-tendering; (D) lifestyle changes, large gifts.
Distractors: (E) Choosing vendors through transparent tenders reduces risk.

FRD-025.q: The sales director's wife owns a distributor that gets the highest discounts. This is:
FRD-025.e: A conflict isn't fraud by itself but is a major opportunity; it must be disclosed and managed.
o: An undisclosed conflict of interest – needs declaration, recusal and independent approval
FRD-025.x:
Basis: ACFE – conflicts of interest; COSO 2013 P1; Law on Enterprises 2020 Arts. 164–167 (disclosure of interests, related persons).
Analysis: The sales director (who sets discounts) has a wife owning the customer with the highest discount → an undisclosed conflict of interest: personal gain may drive decisions to the company's detriment. Remedy: declare it, recuse from related decisions, have discounts approved independently per policy, and review past concessions.
Note: A conflict isn't fraud in itself, but concealing and profiting from it is corruption.

FRD-026.q: Large 'brokerage commissions' to intermediaries of unclear capability, without specific service contracts, in dealings with state customers are a bribery red flag.
FRD-026.e: True. Intermediaries are often used to channel bribes.
FRD-026.x:
Basis: ACFE; UK Bribery Act 2010, US FCPA (intermediary risk); Criminal Code 2015 Art. 364 (offering bribes).
Analysis: True. Large commissions to intermediaries of unclear capability with no specific service contract, especially in dealings with state customers, are a classic bribery channel: the intermediary receives the 'commission' and passes it to officials. Controls: intermediary due diligence (FRD-027), contracts specifying services, evidence of deliverables, market-reasonable fees.

FRD-027.q: Risk-based third-party due diligence before signing an agent in a new market should include:
FRD-027.e: Due diligence depth should match risk (country, industry, transaction type).
o: Verifying beneficial ownership, links to officials, reputation, real capability, anti-bribery and audit-rights clauses
FRD-027.x:
Basis: ACFE; ISO 37001:2016 (due diligence on associates).
Analysis: Risk-based due diligence covers: verifying beneficial owners; links to officials or politically exposed persons; reputation and violation history; real capacity to deliver; contract clauses on anti-bribery, audit rights and termination on breach. Depth matches country, sector and transaction risk.
Distractors: B – a licence says nothing of bribery risk; C – sales staff want a quick signing; D – small agents can still be bribery channels.

FRD-028.q: Select ALL effective gifts and hospitality controls:
FRD-028.e: Verbal notice leaves no evidence and isn't controllable.
o: Clear value thresholds with pre-approval above them
Ban on cash or cash-equivalent gifts
Allow any gift if mentioned verbally
FRD-028.x:
Basis: ACFE; ISO 37001 (gifts and hospitality).
Analysis: Effective measures: (A) clear value thresholds with prior approval above them; (B) a gifts and hospitality register – an auditable trail; (C) banning cash and cash equivalents (gift cards, vouchers) – hard to tell from bribes; (D) banning gifts during tenders and negotiations – the most sensitive periods.
Distractors: (E) Verbal notice leaves no evidence and can't be controlled.

FRD-029.q: An effective data technique to detect conflicts of interest:
FRD-029.e: Data matching is a basic fraud audit tool.
o: Matching employee data (address, phone, bank, relatives) against vendor/customer masters and business registry
FRD-029.x:
Basis: ACFE – data analytics (matching).
Analysis: Matching employee data (address, phone, email, bank account, ID, declared relatives) against vendor and customer masters and business registry data (representatives, shareholders) → reveals conflicts of interest and ghost vendors. Add fuzzy matching (FRD-051).
Distractors: B, C and D can't detect employee–counterparty links.
Note: Processing employees' personal data must comply with data protection law (FRD-072).

FRD-030.q: Small 'facilitation payments' to speed up administrative procedures are accepted under all international anti-corruption frameworks.
FRD-030.e: False. Many frameworks (e.g., the UK Bribery Act) treat them as bribes; Vietnamese law also prohibits giving bribes.
FRD-030.x:
Basis: UK Bribery Act 2010 (no facilitation exception); US FCPA (narrow exception); Anti-Corruption Law 2018; Criminal Code 2015 Art. 364.
Analysis: False. Facilitation payments are bribery under the UK Bribery Act; the US FCPA's exception for routine actions is very narrow and many companies ban them anyway. Vietnamese law prohibits giving bribes in any form; the Criminal Code criminalises bribes from VND 2 million (or less in certain cases). Good corporate policy bans facilitation payments except under threat to personal safety.

FRD-031.q: A construction contractor offers to 'help' renovate the project director's home while quantities are being certified. The main risk to the company:
FRD-031.e: Personal benefits from a counterparty during a decision-making period are a serious conflict.
o: Bribery leading to inflated certification and poor quality – financial and legal damage
FRD-031.x:
Basis: ACFE – corruption; Criminal Code 2015 Arts. 364–365 (giving and taking bribes, including the non-state sector).
Analysis: 'Help' renovating the project director's home while he certifies quantities = a non-cash benefit from a counterparty → bribery/serious conflict. Consequences: fictitious acceptance, inflated quantities, overlooked poor quality → financial loss, structural safety risk and legal exposure (the Code also covers bribery in non-state enterprises).
Distractors: B – it isn't 'private' when the counterparty benefits; C and D aren't the main risk.

FRD-032.q: Select ALL corruption schemes in sales:
FRD-032.e: Selling at approved prices is compliant practice.
o: Salespeople take money to grant discounts/prices beyond policy
Approving credit for weak customers in exchange for benefits
Writing off receivables for personal benefit
FRD-032.x:
Basis: ACFE – corruption in the sales cycle.
Analysis: Schemes: (A) taking money to grant discounts or special prices beyond policy; (B) approving credit for weak customers in exchange for benefits → bad debts; (C) writing off receivables for personal gain; (D) favouring 'cooperative' customers with scarce stock – abusing allocation power.
Distractors: (E) Selling at the approved price list is compliance.

FRD-033.q: Analysis shows 70% of a unit's consulting contracts were direct-awarded to 2 firms that previously shared a legal representative. The appropriate next step:
FRD-033.e: Intangible service contracts (consulting) are easily used to extract cash; check for 'real deliverables'.
o: Verify beneficial ownership, benchmark prices, inspect actual deliverables and approvers
FRD-033.x:
Basis: ACFE – shell companies, conflicts of interest; Law on Bidding 2023 (direct appointment).
Analysis: 70% of a unit's consulting contracts directly awarded to two firms that once shared a legal representative → unusual concentration, possibly front companies. Next: verify beneficial ownership (registry, change history), compare prices with the market, examine actual deliverables (real, valuable, copied?), and who proposed and approved the direct awards.
Distractors: B – evidence is insufficient; C – a contract doesn't prove real services; D acts before verifying.

FRD-034.e: Signs: last-month revenue spikes, large returns next period, fast-growing receivables.
o: Pushing large volumes to distributors at period end with unusual terms or side agreements to return, inflating revenue
FRD-034.x:
Basis: ACFE – financial statement fraud (revenue); VSA 240.
Analysis: Channel stuffing: pushing large volumes to distributors at period-end on unusual terms (deep discounts, extended credit) or side agreements allowing returns → inflating this period's revenue by borrowing from the next. Signs: a last-month revenue spike, large returns early next period (FRD-043), fast-growing receivables, rising distributor inventory.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't this scheme.

FRD-035.q: Select ALL common financial statement fraud schemes:
FRD-035.e: The first five are ACFE's financial statement fraud categories; proper provisioning is compliant practice.
o: Improper asset valuation (no write-downs, improper capitalisation)
Provisioning per standards with full disclosure
FRD-035.x:
Basis: ACFE – FS fraud categories (Fraud Tree).
Analysis: ACFE's five groups: (A) fictitious or premature revenue; (B) concealed liabilities and expenses; (C) improper asset valuations – missing write-downs, wrongly capitalised costs; (D) improper disclosures – related parties, contingent liabilities; (E) timing differences – shifting revenue/expenses between periods.
Distractors: (F) Standards-compliant provisioning with full disclosure is compliance.

FRD-036.q: Earnings quality: net profit VND 150 billion, operating cash flow 30 billion. What is CFO/profit (times)?
FRD-036.e: 30/150 = 0.2 – profit persistently not turning into cash is a red flag, possibly fictitious revenue or improper capitalisation.
FRD-036.x:
Basis: ACFE; FS analysis – earnings quality (accruals).
Working: CFO / net profit = 30 / 150 = 0.2×.
Analysis: Only 20% of profit became cash; the 120 billion of accruals (150 − 30) sits in receivables, inventory, capitalised assets… If persistent, it's a warning: fictitious/early revenue (rising receivables), wrongly capitalised costs, inflated inventory. Fast growers can legitimately show low CFO → look at the trend and explanations.
Check: 150 × 0.2 = 30 ✓.

FRD-037.q: An entity keeps capitalising rapidly rising 'software development costs' while expensed R&D falls and profit rises. The risk:
FRD-037.e: Test development-phase criteria (technical feasibility, intent, ability to generate benefits, reliable measurement).
o: Improper capitalisation of costs not meeting intangible asset criteria to inflate profit
FRD-037.x:
Basis: VAS 04 para 41 (recognising development-phase intangibles); IAS 38 para 57.
Analysis: Rapidly rising capitalised development costs while expensed R&D falls and profit rises → risk of capitalising costs that don't qualify (research phase, or development not meeting the six criteria) to inflate profit and assets. Test: technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete and use/sell, how future benefits arise, resources, reliable cost measurement.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

FRD-038.q: 'Round-tripping' (sell and buy back) with related or colluding parties inflates revenue without economic substance.
FRD-038.e: True. Revenue and costs (or assets) rise together while cash goes in a circle.
FRD-038.x:
Basis: ACFE – fictitious revenue (round-tripping); VSA 550.
Analysis: True. Round-tripping: selling to a counterparty (often related or under a side deal) and buying back equivalent goods, services or assets, or returning the cash → revenue and costs (or assets) rise together while money circles back, with no economic substance. Aim: inflating revenue, scale and growth.

FRD-039.q: Select ALL financial statement fraud red flags (per VSA 240 and practice):
FRD-039.e: Prudent, stable policies are a positive sign.
o: Profit growth far above industry with negative operating cash flow
Large complex transactions near period end
Frequent auditor changes, disputes with auditors
Excessive management involvement in policies and estimates
Management bonuses tightly tied to short-term profit
FRD-039.x:
Basis: VSA 240 appendix 1 (fraudulent reporting risk factors).
Analysis: Warning signs: (A) profit growth beating the industry with negative operating cash flow (FRD-036); (B) large, complex transactions near period-end; (C) frequent auditor changes, disputes with auditors; (D) management over-involved in policies and estimates; (E) bonuses tightly tied to short-term profit – pressure.
Distractors: (F) Conservative, stable policies over many years are a positive sign.

FRD-040.e: Earnings smoothing is financial statement fraud even if multi-year totals are unchanged.
o: Over-providing in good years and releasing in bad years to smooth earnings
FRD-040.x:
Basis: ACFE – FS fraud (timing differences, improper reserves); SEC – 'earnings management'.
Analysis: Cookie-jar reserves: over-providing (warranty, bad debts, restructuring) in strong years → 'storing' profit; releasing it in weak years to dress up results. Multi-year total profit may be unchanged but each period is misstated → still FS fraud, hiding the business's true volatility.
Distractors: B, C and D are other schemes.

FRD-041.q: Beneish's DSRI = (Receivables/Sales this year) / (Receivables/Sales last year). Last year AR 100, sales 1,000; this year AR 180, sales 1,200. What is DSRI (2 decimals)?
FRD-041.e: (180/1,200) / (100/1,000) = 0.15/0.10 = 1.50 → receivables grow faster than sales, signalling possible revenue inflation.
FRD-041.x:
Basis: Beneish (1999), 'The Detection of Earnings Manipulation', Financial Analysts Journal.
Working: DSRI = (180 / 1,200) / (100 / 1,000) = 0.15 / 0.10 = 1.50.
Analysis: DSRI > 1 means receivables grew faster than sales (sales +20%, receivables +80%) → possible inflated revenue or looser credit. In Beneish's study, manipulators averaged a DSRI of about 1.46 versus about 1.03 for non-manipulators.
Check: equivalent days of receivables 54.75 versus 36.5 (×1.5) ✓.

FRD-042.q: A typical scheme to conceal liabilities is:
FRD-042.e: Searches for unrecorded liabilities and bank confirmations (guarantees) are suitable responses.
o: Not recording period-end invoices, not accruing, hiding guarantees and commitments
FRD-042.x:
Basis: ACFE – concealed liabilities and expenses; VSA 500, VSA 505.
Analysis: Concealment tactics: not recording year-end supplier invoices (kept in a drawer), not accruing incurred costs, omitting warranty or litigation provisions, hiding guarantees and commitments → lower expenses and liabilities, higher profit. Audit response: search for unrecorded liabilities via post-year-end payments and invoices (AUD-035), bank confirmations of guarantees (AUD-043), lawyers' letters.
Distractors: B, C and D lower profit or are proper practice.

FRD-043.q: A revenue spike in the last 2 weeks of the year with large credit notes/returns in January is a strong sign of cut-off fraud or fictitious revenue.
FRD-043.e: True. Test delivery documents, return terms and side agreements.
FRD-043.x:
Basis: VSA 240 appendices 2–3; ACFE (FRD-034).
Analysis: True. A revenue spike in the last two weeks with large credit notes and returns in January → fictitious or premature revenue reversed into the next period (cut-off, channel stuffing). Procedures: check customer-signed delivery notes and bills of lading; return terms; confirm side agreements directly with customers (AUD-044).

FRD-044.q: A developer records revenue when buyers sign 10% deposit contracts, with apartments unfinished and not handed over. This is:
FRD-044.e: Deposits are liabilities (customer advances) until recognition criteria are met.
o: Premature revenue – contrary to VAS 14/IFRS 15 on transfer of control
FRD-044.x:
Basis: VAS 14 para 10 (sale-of-goods recognition criteria); IFRS 15 paras 31–38; Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (customer advances).
Analysis: Recognising revenue when buyers sign a 10% deposit contract, with the apartment unbuilt and not handed over → risks and rewards/control haven't passed → premature revenue in breach of the standards. Deposits are liabilities (customer advances) until handover (ICA-075).
Note: Under IFRS 15, some off-plan apartment contracts may qualify for over-time recognition under para 35(c), depending on contract law; that never justifies booking all revenue at deposit.

FRD-045.q: Select ALL audit responses to revenue fraud risk:
FRD-045.e: Tax returns are prepared by the entity itself and not independent for fraud detection.
o: Disaggregated analytics by month, product, customer
Confirming contract terms (return rights, side deals) with customers
Thorough cut-off testing around period end
Interviewing sales and warehouse staff about unusual period-end deals
Only agreeing total revenue to tax returns
FRD-045.x:
Basis: VSA 240 paras 26, 30, appendix 2.
Analysis: Responses to revenue fraud risk: (A) detailed analytics by month, product, customer and channel – spotting period-end anomalies; (B) confirming contract terms with customers – return rights, side agreements, delivery terms; (C) rigorous cut-off testing around year-end; (D) interviewing sales and warehouse staff – people outside accounting often know of unusual deals.
Distractors: (E) Tax returns are prepared by the entity, not independent, and only mirror what was recorded.

FRD-046.q: Fictitious inventory can be concealed at counts by:
FRD-046.e: Responses: simultaneous counts, surprise box checks, control of count-sheet numbering.
o: Moving goods between sites counted on different days, empty boxes stacked inside, adding count sheets later
FRD-046.x:
Basis: VSA 501; ACFE – concealing fictitious inventory.
Analysis: Count-time tricks: moving goods between sites counted on different days (one batch counted twice); hollow stacks with empty boxes inside; adding count tags afterwards; misstating specs or quality; claiming fictitious goods in transit or on consignment. Responses: simultaneous counts across sites, surprise opening of packages, tag-number control, photos, test counts from records to floor.
Distractors: B, C and D are good controls.

FRD-047.q: Under Benford's Law, the probability that the first digit is '1' in natural datasets is approximately:
FRD-047.x:
Basis: Benford's Law (Newcomb 1881; Benford 1938); Nigrini – Forensic Analytics.
Working: P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d); P(1) = log10(2) ≈ 0.3010 = 30.1%.
Analysis: In natural data spanning several orders of magnitude, small leading digits dominate: '1' ≈ 30.1%, '2' ≈ 17.6%, … '9' ≈ 4.6%. Significant deviation may indicate invented or altered data.
Distractors: B – 11.1% (1/9) is a uniform distribution; C is baseless; D – 4.6% is the probability of '9'.

FRD-048.q: Under Benford's Law, what is the probability that the first digit is '9' (%, 1 decimal)?
FRD-048.x:
Basis: Benford's Law.
Working: P(9) = log10(1 + 1/9) = log10(10/9) = log10(1.1111) ≈ 0.0458 ≈ 4.6%.
Check: The sum of P(1)…P(9) = log10(2/1 × 3/2 × … × 10/9) = log10(10) = 1 ✓ – a complete distribution.
Analysis: An unusually high share of amounts starting with '9' (say 15%) may reflect transactions made just under approval limits (90–99 million – FRD-014).

FRD-049.q: Benford's Law suits all datasets, including sequential invoice numbers and fixed prices.
FRD-049.e: False. It doesn't apply to assigned numbers, bounded data or fixed prices; it suits natural transaction data spanning orders of magnitude.
FRD-049.x:
Basis: Nigrini – Benford's Law: Applications for Forensic Accounting (conditions of use).
Analysis: False. Benford doesn't apply to: assigned numbers (sequential invoice numbers, employee IDs, phone numbers); data with narrow min/max (advance limits of 5–10 million); fixed prices or rule-driven amounts (flat fees); small datasets. It suits natural transactional data spanning several magnitudes and large enough (typically thousands of records) – e.g., vendor payment amounts, invoice-level sales.

FRD-050.q: Select ALL fraud analytics tests in procure-to-pay:
FRD-050.e: Regional revenue is a sales analysis, not procure-to-pay.
o: Duplicate payments (same vendor, amount, similar invoice numbers)
Incomplete vendor records, newly created and paid immediately
Payments on holidays or after hours
FRD-050.x:
Basis: ACFE – fraud data analytics (procure-to-pay).
Analysis: P2P tests: (A) duplicate payments – same vendor and amount, near-identical invoice numbers (extra characters, transposed digits); (B) new vendors with incomplete files paid immediately (FRD-085); (C) invoices just under approval limits (FRD-014); (D) weekend or after-hours payments; (E) unusually round amounts (FRD-095).
Distractors: (F) Revenue by region belongs to the sales cycle.

FRD-051.e: Perpetrators often create look-alike vendors to evade exact-match tests.
o: Find vendor names/addresses that are near-duplicates or resemble employees (e.g., 'ABC Co' vs 'A.B.C Company')
FRD-051.x:
Basis: ACFE – fraud data analytics (fuzzy matching); Nigrini – Forensic Analytics.
Analysis: Fuzzy matching uses string-distance algorithms (Levenshtein, Soundex, normalising diacritics, punctuation and words like 'Company/Co./Ltd') to catch near-identical names and addresses: 'ABC Co' – 'A.B.C Company'; vendors resembling employee names. Fraudsters create slightly altered duplicates to evade exact-match tests.
Distractors: B, C and D are ordinary data operations.

FRD-052.q: A gap test on sales invoice numbers 0001 to 5000 finds 4,950 recorded. How many missing invoices need explaining?
FRD-052.e: 5,000 − 4,950 = 50 – possibly valid voids or revenue kept off the books.
FRD-052.x:
Basis: ACFE – gap testing (document sequence); Decree 123/2020/ND-CP (e-invoices – cancelled and erroneous invoices).
Working: Missing invoices = 5,000 − 4,950 = 50 (the range 0001–5000 holds 5,000 numbers).
Analysis: Each gap must be explained by valid cancellation records (cancellation notices, minutes, status on the tax authority's e-invoice system); unexplained gaps may be off-book revenue (invoices issued but not recorded – a completeness/skimming risk).
Check: 4,950 + 50 = 5,000 ✓.

FRD-053.q: Internal audit finds 2% of GL entries posted after close by the chief accountant's account, mostly Dr Receivables / Cr Revenue, round sums. The right approach:
FRD-053.e: Post-close, round-sum revenue entries are classic management override features.
o: Treat as high risk; inspect documents, approvals and substance of each entry, and interview independently
Ignore it since the chief accountant has rights
FRD-053.x:
Basis: VSA 240 para 32a, A41–A44; ACFE.
Analysis: Post-close entries by the chief accountant's account, Dr receivables/Cr revenue, round amounts → many hallmarks of override (AUD-050): a powerful user, period-end timing, revenue accounts, round numbers. Approach: treat as high risk; examine source documents, approvals and substance of each entry; confirm related receivables; interview others independently; check whether the account is shared.
Distractors: B – authority doesn't make entries valid; C – entries can't just be deleted; D – asking the preparer isn't independent.

FRD-054.q: Select ALL data tests for payroll fraud:
FRD-054.e: Birthdays are unrelated to fraud risk.
o: Employees sharing bank accounts, ID numbers, addresses
FRD-054.x:
Basis: ACFE – payroll fraud analytics (FRD-016).
Analysis: Payroll tests: (A) shared bank accounts, IDs or addresses among staff – ghosts, money to one person; (B) pay without attendance data – people not working; (C) never taking leave – a concealment signal (or a non-existent employee); (D) pay changes without decisions – unauthorised raises.
Distractors: (E) Birth month has nothing to do with fraud risk.
Note: Processing ID numbers and personal data must comply with data protection law (FRD-072).

FRD-055.q: Exceptions from data analytics are only red flags to investigate, not proof of fraud.
FRD-055.e: True. Many exceptions have valid explanations; documents and context must be checked.
FRD-055.x:
Basis: ACFE; IIA GIAS 2024 (evaluating evidence).
Analysis: True. Analytics exceptions are only red flags – many have legitimate explanations (two equal instalments looking like duplicates, spouses sharing an account under valid authorisation). Check documents and context and interview before concluding; hasty conclusions create legal risk and harm innocent people (AUD-061).

FRD-056.q: A restaurant chain's POS analysis shows one cashier's post-print void rate is 8x average. The suspected scheme:
FRD-056.e: Match against CCTV and require shift-manager approval of every void.
o: Collecting cash then voiding the POS sale to pocket it (void fraud)
FRD-056.x:
Basis: ACFE – register disbursement schemes (void fraud); ICA-060.
Analysis: Post-receipt voids at 8× the average → suspected void fraud: the cashier collects payment against a printed bill, then voids it on the POS → recorded sales drop and the matching cash is taken. Controls: every void approved with the shift manager's own code; void exception reports by cashier; CCTV matching; encourage customers to take e-invoices.
Distractors: B, C and D can't explain an anomaly concentrated in one person.

FRD-057.q: A duplicate-payment test flags 30 suspected pairs worth VND 450 million; after verification 60% of the amount is genuinely duplicated. How much should be recovered from vendors (VND million)?
FRD-057.x:
Basis: ACFE – duplicate payment testing.
Working: Genuine duplicates = 450 × 60% = VND 270 million.
Analysis: The other 40% (180 million) are false positives (valid pairs with similar features). The 270 million should be recovered or offset from vendors, and the cause found (system error, a failing duplicate block – AUD-024, or intent – FRD-082) and controls fixed.
Check: 270 + 180 = 450 ✓.

FRD-058.q: To detect fictitious revenue at a distributor, the most useful analytics:
FRD-058.e: Fictitious revenue usually lacks matching flows of goods and cash.
o: Match sales invoices to shipping documents, warehouse issues and cash; find new high-volume customers that never pay
FRD-058.x:
Basis: ACFE; VSA 240.
Analysis: Fictitious revenue usually lacks matching goods and cash flows. The most useful analysis: three-way matching of sales invoices – shipping and goods-issue documents – cash receipts; find invoices with no issue or shipment; new customers with big sales but no payments and ageing balances; customers sharing data with employees or related parties.
Distractors: B, C and D don't bear directly on whether revenue is real.

FRD-059.q: Consider these statements on fraud analytics:
FRD-059.e: Process understanding is needed to design meaningful tests and interpret exceptions.
o: Testing 100% of the population avoids sampling risk.
Source data quality directly affects reliability of results.
No understanding of business processes is needed for analytics.
Periodic tests (continuous monitoring) should be set up for key risks.
FRD-059.x:
Basis: ACFE; IIA (GTAG – Data Analysis Technologies).
Analysis: True – analysing 100% removes sampling risk (ICA-084). True – poor source data (missing, wrong, duplicated) makes results unreliable, so test completeness and accuracy first (AUD-066). False – understanding the business process is essential to design meaningful tests and interpret exceptions. True – continuous monitoring of key risks enables early detection.

FRD-060.q: Return-rate analysis by salesperson shows one with 25% returns versus a 3% average, mostly early the next month. The most plausible hypothesis:
FRD-060.e: A month-end/month-start pattern tied to KPIs is a classic sign.
o: The salesperson books fake month-end sales to hit KPIs, then raises returns
FRD-060.x:
Basis: ACFE – fictitious sales tied to KPIs.
Analysis: One salesperson with 25% returns versus a 3% average, concentrated early next month → a timing pattern tied to the KPI period: booking fake month-end sales to hit targets and earn bonuses, then reversing via returns. Controls: KPIs on net sales after returns, bonus clawbacks (ICA-094), independent return approval, checking returned goods actually re-enter stock.
Distractors: B – a system-wide quality issue wouldn't be confined to one person; C and D don't explain the timing pattern.

FRD-061.q: Which fraud prevention measure directly reduces 'opportunity'?
FRD-061.e: Raising the perceived likelihood of detection is the strongest deterrent.
o: Segregation of duties, system access rights, surprise counts, regular analytics
FRD-061.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P10; Cressey (FRD-002).
Analysis: 'Opportunity' is cut directly by controls: segregation, system access rights, surprise counts, regular data analytics. ACFE notes the perception of detection is the strongest deterrent.
Distractors: B – pay rises affect pressure/rationalisation, not opportunity; C – ethics training targets rationalisation; D is irrelevant.

FRD-062.q: Select ALL features of an effective whistleblowing channel:
FRD-062.e: Requiring signatures reduces reports out of fear of retaliation.
o: Multiple channels (phone, web, email), anonymity allowed
Run independently of management (third party or reporting to the Audit Committee)
FRD-062.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P14; ISO 37002:2021 (whistleblowing management systems).
Analysis: Effective hotlines: (A) multiple channels allowing anonymity; (B) independent of management – a third party or direct reporting to the audit committee; (C) a clear anti-retaliation policy; (D) feedback to reporters on progress (without sensitive detail) – building trust (ICA-079).
Distractors: (E) Requiring names reduces reports through fear of retaliation.

FRD-063.q: Arrange the internal fraud investigation process:
FRD-063.e: Interview the suspect last to avoid evidence destruction and to have enough to confront.
o: Plan the investigation, scope and team (with legal)
Collect and analyse documentary and data evidence
FRD-063.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual (Investigation – interview theory).
Analysis: Order: (1) receive and preliminarily assess the information's credibility; (2) plan scope and team, including legal; (3) preserve evidence – data, email, documents – before destruction; (4) gather and analyse documentary and data evidence; (5) interview from neutral witnesses to involved parties, the suspect last; (6) report findings and recommendations.
Note: Interviewing the suspect last prevents evidence destruction and provides grounds for confrontation.

FRD-064.q: In fraud investigations, chain of custody must be maintained for evidence to be legally valid.
FRD-064.e: True. Record who collected it, when and how it was stored; for electronic data, use forensic images.
FRD-064.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual; Criminal Procedure Code 2015 (collecting and preserving evidence, electronic data).
Analysis: True. Chain of custody records who collected evidence, when, where, to whom it passed and how it was stored → proving it wasn't altered and preserving legal value for prosecutors or labour disputes. For electronic data: forensic images and hash values prove integrity; never work on the original.

FRD-065.q: Correct principles when interviewing a fraud suspect:
FRD-065.e: Coerced admissions may be invalid and create legal risk for the company.
o: At least two interviewers, questions from general to specific, no threats or promises, documented
Interview alone to put them at ease
Threaten police to force a confession
Record secretly in breach of law
FRD-065.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual (Interviewing); Labour Code 2019 (disciplinary process – employee rights).
Analysis: Principles: at least two interviewers (one asks, one records and witnesses); questions from general to specific; no threats, promises or detention; written minutes signed by the interviewee; recordings only lawfully (notice, consent). Coerced admissions may be worthless and expose the company to claims.
Distractors: B lacks a witness; C – threats are coercion; D is unlawful.

FRD-066.q: Select ALL immediate steps when serious fraud by a manager is suspected:
FRD-066.e: Announcing before verification may breach personal rights and compromise the investigation.
o: Restrict the suspect's system and asset access
Consult legal on reporting duties and employee rights
FRD-066.x:
Basis: ACFE; Labour Code 2019 Art. 128 (temporary suspension); data protection law.
Analysis: On serious suspicion: (A) restrict the suspect's system and asset access (possibly suspending them under the Labour Code) – preventing further loss and wiping of traces; (B) preserve email, data and documents; (C) inform the audit committee/board; (D) consult legal on reporting duties and employee rights.
Distractors: (E) Naming someone before verification may breach personal rights, invite defamation claims and tip off others, spoiling the investigation.

FRD-067.q: Fraud losses are quantified for a fidelity insurance claim. The most important requirement:
FRD-067.e: Many fidelity policies have short notification deadlines after discovery.
o: Document-supported loss quantification, separating direct loss from investigation costs, meeting the policy's notice deadlines
Including lost expected profit not covered
Waiting for the criminal case to end before notifying
FRD-067.x:
Basis: ACFE; employee fidelity/crime insurance practice.
Analysis: A claim needs: documented loss quantification (tracing each transaction); separating direct loss (stolen cash and assets) from investigation costs (covered only if the policy says so); meeting the notice deadline from discovery and the proof-of-loss deadline.
Distractors: B – guesswork gets rejected; C – lost expected profit is usually excluded; D – waiting for the criminal case may breach notice terms and forfeit cover.

FRD-068.q: Mandatory consecutive leave (e.g., at least 1–2 weeks/year) for sensitive roles helps detect frauds requiring daily concealment.
FRD-068.e: True. Stand-ins may spot anomalies like lapping.
FRD-068.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P10.
Analysis: True. Many schemes (lapping, master data change-and-revert, hiding stock shortages) need daily upkeep by the perpetrator. Mandatory 1–2 week continuous leave with someone else covering the job → the concealment chain breaks and the cover spots anomalies (customers querying balances, mismatched credits). It works best when the cover genuinely does the work and the absent person's accounts are locked.

FRD-069.q: A comprehensive fraud risk management programme (per COSO/ACFE guidance) has five components: governance, risk assessment, prevention, detection and:
FRD-069.e: The COSO/ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide aligns with the 17 COSO 2013 principles.
o: Investigation and corrective action, with programme monitoring
FRD-069.x:
Basis: COSO/ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide (2016, 2nd ed. 2023).
Analysis: The guide has five principles: (1) fraud risk governance; (2) fraud risk assessment; (3) preventive and detective control activities; (4) investigation and corrective action; (5) monitoring. They map to COSO 2013's 17 principles, especially P8 (ICA-013).
Note: The guide combines prevention and detection into one principle; the question lists them separately, but the answer's substance (investigation and corrective action, plus monitoring) is correct.

FRD-070.q: After resolving a procurement fraud, the most important step to prevent recurrence:
FRD-070.e: Without fixing the control gap, others may repeat it.
o: Root-cause analysis (which control failed and why), fix control design and review similar processes
FRD-070.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P17 (ICA-097).
Analysis: Disciplining one person leaves the control gap open for others. The key step: root-cause analysis – which controls failed (design or operation) and why it wasn't caught sooner; redesign controls; review similar processes and units for the same gap; update the fraud risk assessment.
Distractors: B treats symptoms only; C loses the deterrent effect (ICA-086); D doesn't address opportunity.

FRD-071.q: Select ALL fraud prevention measures when hiring for sensitive roles (cashier, procurement, AP):
FRD-071.e: Pre-employment checks must comply with personal data laws.
o: Sign confidentiality, code of conduct, conflict declarations
FRD-071.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P4; data protection law (FRD-072).
Analysis: Hiring for sensitive roles: (A) verify background, qualifications and experience – catching fake credentials; (B) contact previous employers' references – learning of fraud-related exits; (C) sign confidentiality, code of conduct and conflict-of-interest declarations; (D) supervised probation with limited access rights.
Distractors: (E) Skipping checks to hire quickly raises risk.
Note: Collecting candidate information requires consent and purpose limitation under data protection law.

FRD-072.q: Under Vietnamese personal data protection law, a company investigating fraud must still process data lawfully, for a clear purpose and only to the extent necessary.
FRD-072.e: True. Collecting staff emails and data requires a legal basis (internal rules, employment contracts, consent, etc.).
FRD-072.x:
Basis: Decree 13/2023/ND-CP on personal data protection; Personal Data Protection Law 2025 (to my knowledge effective 1 Jan 2026 – check the original and implementing guidance).
Analysis: True. Fraud investigations don't exempt data protection duties: processing needs a legal basis (internal rules, employment contracts, consent, or statutory no-consent cases), a clear purpose, minimal scope (only case-relevant data), security and limited retention. Access to company email should be pre-authorised in IT usage rules.

FRD-073.q: Which control prevents staff from using pre-signed cheques/payment orders to transfer funds?
FRD-073.e: Maker and approver tokens must be held by different people.
o: No blank signing; dual signatures with the second checking source documents; e-banking with separate maker/checker rights
Keep payment orders in a drawer
One person holds both maker and approver tokens
FRD-073.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10; e-banking control practice.
Analysis: Controls: never pre-sign cheques or payment orders; dual signatures, with the second signer checking source documents (PO, invoice, payment request) first; e-banking with separate maker and checker rights, tokens held by two different people, and transaction limits.
Distractors: B – signed forms in a drawer create opportunity; C – one person holding maker and checker tokens defeats segregation; D – year-end checking is too late.

FRD-074.q: A manufacturer finds scrap sales abnormally low versus material usage standards. Suspected scheme:
FRD-074.e: A material balance (input – output – scrap – loss) is the key test.
o: Scrap or good material sold off-book, or understated scrap weights/prices
Slight drop in market scrap prices
FRD-074.x:
Basis: ACFE – inventory/scrap schemes.
Analysis: Scrap sales unusually low relative to consumption standards → scrap (or good material declared as scrap) sold outside without recording, or quantities and prices under-declared (colluding with buyers). Key test: material balance – issued = finished-goods equivalent + scrap + normal loss (FRD-075); controls: independently witnessed scrap weighing, auctioned scrap sales.
Distractors: B, C and D don't explain the gap (a slight price fall doesn't reduce volume).

FRD-075.q: Material balance: 1,000 tonnes of steel issued; finished goods equivalent 900 tonnes; standard scrap 6%; standard loss 1%. Recorded scrap sales are 30 tonnes. How many tonnes of scrap are unexplained?
FRD-075.e: Expected scrap = 1,000 × 6% = 60 tonnes; recorded 30 → 30 tonnes short. Also 900 + 60 + 10 = 970, leaving 30 tonnes on hand or lost to explain.
FRD-075.x:
Basis: ACFE; material balance analysis.
Working: Expected scrap = 1,000 × 6% = 60 tonnes; recorded sales 30 → unexplained scrap gap = 60 − 30 = 30 tonnes.
Balance check: finished 900 + standard scrap 60 + standard loss 10 = 970 → 30 tonnes beyond standards (unprocessed stock or leakage). Using recorded scrap: 1,000 − 900 − 30 − 10 = 60 tonnes unexplained in total.
Analysis: Count scrap on hand, check weighbridge slips and scrap sales contracts, compare standards across shifts/workshops.

FRD-076.q: A pharma company sponsors doctors' conferences at resorts, including family travel. The main risk:
FRD-076.e: Sponsorship must have a scientific purpose, reasonable value, transparency and sector compliance.
o: Commercial bribery/improper influence on prescribing; breaches of promotion and anti-corruption rules
FRD-076.x:
Basis: ACFE – corruption; Pharmacy Law 2016, Advertising Law (drug information and promotion); industry ethics (IFPMA Code).
Analysis: Sponsoring a resort conference with travel for doctors' families → personal benefit beyond scientific purpose → commercial bribery and improper influence on prescribing; breaches of drug promotion rules and anti-corruption law (public-hospital doctors hold official positions). Legitimate sponsorship: scientific purpose, suitable venue, reasonable costs, attendees only, transparency.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main risk.

FRD-077.q: Management books 3-year bundled software service revenue upfront at signing. Scheme and audit response:
FRD-077.e: Services delivered over time are recognised over time.
o: Premature revenue; test performance obligations, defer unearned revenue, recognise over the service period
FRD-077.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 22, 35, B58–B63; VAS 14 para 16 (services by stage of completion).
Analysis: A 3-year software service contract – services delivered over time (the customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits) → revenue recognised over 3 years; booking all at signing is premature. Audit response: identify performance obligations (licence, hosting, support, updates), allocate the price, move the unearned part to deferred revenue and recognise it over time.
Distractors: B breaches the standards; C – confirmations don't fix timing; D misstates the nature.

FRD-078.q: Select ALL red flags of undisclosed related-party fraud:
FRD-078.e: Open competitive tenders are a positive sign.
o: New customers/suppliers with sudden large deals, addresses matching shareholders' offices
Complex transactions near period end without clear business purpose
Large receivables 'collected' using funds lent by related parties
Transactions via open tenders with many independent bidders
FRD-078.x:
Basis: VSA 550 para A23 (indicators of undisclosed related parties); ACFE.
Analysis: Indicators: (A) new customers/vendors with sudden large volumes and addresses matching a shareholder's office; (B) complex, purpose-unclear deals near period-end; (C) large receivables 'collected' with money borrowed from related parties – circular cash hiding bad debts; (D) interest-free, unsecured loans – off-market terms.
Distractors: (E) Open tenders with many independent bidders are a positive sign.

FRD-079.q: An SME can't afford an internal audit function. A cost-effective anti-fraud approach:
FRD-079.e: Direct owner oversight is an important compensating control.
o: Owner reviews bank statements, approves new vendors, does surprise counts; co-source thematic internal audits
Rely only on the year-end FS audit
FRD-079.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (smaller entities – compensating controls); ACFE (small businesses suffer proportionally large losses).
Analysis: Small firms lacking staff for segregation → direct owner oversight is a cost-effective compensating control (ICA-021): personally receiving and reviewing original bank statements, approving new vendors and bank detail changes, surprise counts, approving large payments; outsourcing targeted internal audits.
Distractors: B and C leave controls empty; D – an FS audit isn't designed to catch all fraud (FRD-080).

FRD-080.q: The annual FS audit is mainly designed to detect all fraud, including small employee frauds.
FRD-080.e: False. FS audits target material misstatement; per ACFE, external audit is not a primary fraud detection method.
FRD-080.x:
Basis: VSA 200 para 5, A51–A52; VSA 240 paras 5–6; ACFE Report to the Nations.
Analysis: False. An FS audit seeks reasonable assurance that the FS are free of material misstatement; it isn't designed to detect all fraud, especially small, collusive or cleverly concealed schemes. ACFE finds external audits detect only a small share (about 3–4%) of occupational frauds, far below tips (FRD-004).

FRD-081.q: A common recent external fraud against businesses is:
FRD-081.e: Prevention: independent call-backs, awareness training, strict transfer approval.
o: Spoofed executive/supplier emails requesting transfers (CEO fraud/BEC), fake invoices
FRD-081.x:
Basis: ACFE; FBI IC3 Internet Crime Report (BEC); ICA-046.
Analysis: Common external frauds: spoofed executive emails (CEO fraud) demanding urgent, confidential transfers; spoofed supplier emails (BEC) announcing new bank details; fake invoices. Prevention: verify via stored independent channels (call the number on file), training to spot fake emails (look-alike domains), strict transfer approval, never bypassing procedure even for 'orders from the boss'.
Distractors: B, C and D are internal frauds.

FRD-082.q: An AP clerk deliberately double-pays, then asks the vendor to refund to a personal account. Detective controls:
FRD-082.e: Unusual debit balances in payables (overpayments) are a red flag.
o: Central tracking of vendor refunds/debit balances; refunds only to company accounts; independent vendor reconciliations
Let the AP clerk handle refunds
FRD-082.x:
Basis: ACFE – billing schemes (overpayment and refund diversion).
Analysis: Scheme: deliberately paying twice, then asking the vendor to refund the overpayment into a personal account. Trace: unusual debit balances (overpayments) on the vendor's payables account. Detective controls: central monitoring of refunds and payables debit balances, reviewed independently; a policy that refunds go only to company accounts; independent periodic vendor statement reconciliation; duplicate payment tests (FRD-057).
Distractors: B, C and D create opportunity.

FRD-083.q: Consider these statements on occupational fraud:
FRD-083.e: Per ACFE reports, most perpetrators have no prior fraud convictions.
o: The longer a fraud lasts, the bigger the loss.
Most perpetrators have prior fraud convictions.
Weak or missing controls are a common enabling factor.
Small businesses often suffer relatively large losses due to weak controls.
FRD-083.x:
Basis: ACFE Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations.
Analysis: True – longer schemes cause bigger losses (median duration before detection about 12 months). False – most perpetrators (about 85–90%) had no prior fraud conviction or sanction → background checks aren't enough. True – lack of controls and override are the most common enabling factors. True – organisations under 100 staff suffer median dollar losses not far below large ones, so the impact relative to their size is heavier.
Note: Percentages vary by edition.

FRD-084.q: The Beneish M-score is used to:
FRD-084.e: Altman's Z-score predicts bankruptcy; the M-score screens for earnings manipulation.
o: Estimate the probability of earnings manipulation from financial ratios
FRD-084.x:
Basis: Beneish (1999), Financial Analysts Journal; Altman (1968) – Z-score.
Analysis: The M-score (8 variables: DSRI, GMI, AQI, SGI, DEPI, SGAI, LVGI, TATA) estimates the likelihood of earnings manipulation; a common cut-off is −1.78 (8-variable model): M > −1.78 → higher likelihood. It's a screen, not proof.
Distractors: B – Altman's Z-score predicts bankruptcy; C and D are unrelated.

FRD-085.q: Analysis of vendor creation vs first payment dates: 12 vendors created and paid the same day, by the same creator and approver. Assessment:
FRD-085.e: Create-and-pay-immediately by the same person is a classic risk combination.
o: High risk of ghost vendors and SoD conflicts; check legal records, delivery documents and links to staff
FRD-085.x:
Basis: ACFE – fraud analytics (vendor master); COSO 2013 P10–11 (ICA-085).
Analysis: 12 vendors created and paid the same day by the same creator and approver → the classic risk combination: conflicting rights (create vendor + approve payment), no time for vetting, ghost-vendor risk. Procedures: check legal files (tax code, registration), delivery/acceptance documents, matching against employee data (FRD-029), and remove the conflicting rights.
Distractors: B, C and D ignore the red flag.

FRD-086.q: Select ALL items an anti-fraud policy should include:
FRD-086.e: Companies may have legal duties to report crimes.
o: Definition of fraud and prohibited conduct
Responsibilities of the Board, management, staff and internal audit
A pledge never to report to authorities
FRD-086.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013; Criminal Code 2015 Arts. 19, 390 (failing to report crimes); Anti-Corruption Law 2018.
Analysis: An anti-fraud policy should include: (A) definitions and prohibited conduct; (B) responsibilities of the board, management, staff and IA; (C) reporting channels and whistleblower protection (FRD-062); (D) investigation procedure (FRD-063) and consistent discipline.
Distractors: (E) Promising never to report to authorities may conflict with legal duties (individuals may be liable for failing to report crimes in some cases) and destroys deterrence.

FRD-087.q: ISO 37001 guides organisations in establishing an anti-bribery management system.
FRD-087.e: True. It can be independently certified.
FRD-087.x:
Basis: ISO 37001:2016 – Anti-bribery management systems.
Analysis: True. ISO 37001 sets requirements and guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and improving an anti-bribery management system: policy, leadership, bribery risk assessment, due diligence (FRD-027), financial and non-financial controls, gifts (FRD-028), reporting channels and investigations. Organisations can be certified by an independent third party.
Note: Certification doesn't guarantee the absence of bribery.

FRD-088.q: A builder with many sites pays seasonal workers cash via team leaders. Main risk and controls:
FRD-088.e: Cash payment via intermediaries is a major fraud opportunity.
o: Ghost workers, inflated days; controls: biometric/photo attendance on site, ID checks, pay into workers' own accounts, surprise checks
FRD-088.x:
Basis: ACFE – payroll schemes; COSO 2013 P10; Labour Code 2019 Art. 96 (paying wages directly to employees).
Analysis: Cash wages paid via team leaders to casual workers on many sites → ghost workers, padded days, leaders skimming pay. Controls: biometric/geotagged photo attendance on site; ID checks; paying into each worker's own account (the Labour Code requires direct, full payment); surprise headcounts on site.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main risk.

FRD-089.q: ERP login analysis shows an employee on leave still approving payments. This indicates:
FRD-089.e: Need MFA, no account sharing and formal delegation during absences.
o: Password sharing/unauthorised account use – undermining access controls
FRD-089.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (5.17 authentication information, 8.5 secure authentication).
Analysis: An account of someone on leave still approving payments → someone else is using it (shared or stolen password) → access and approval controls are void: the real approver is unknown, and one person may prepare and 'approve' with another's account. Fix: MFA, a ban on account sharing, formal in-system delegation during absence, monitoring of unusual logins.
Distractors: B, C and D misread the issue.

FRD-090.q: Signs of 'fictitious assets' in supplier advances:
FRD-090.e: Advances are often used to extract cash to related parties.
o: Large advances outstanding for many periods, no deliveries, related-party links, no security
Advances under contracts with bank guarantees
FRD-090.x:
Basis: ACFE; VSA 550; Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (advances to suppliers).
Analysis: Signs of fictitious prepayments/cash extraction: large advances outstanding for several periods; no delivery or refund; the counterparty is related; no guarantee or collateral; vague contracts. It's a common channel for moving cash to related parties while keeping an 'asset' on the balance sheet.
Distractors: B, C and D describe well-controlled advances.

FRD-091.q: Select ALL metrics measuring anti-fraud programme effectiveness:
FRD-091.e: Document counts don't reflect real effectiveness.
o: Number and quality of tips, handling time
Share of staff completing training and sign-off
Share detected by proactive controls vs by accident
FRD-091.x:
Basis: COSO/ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide (principle 5 – monitoring).
Analysis: Meaningful metrics: (A) volume and quality of tips (substantiation rate) and resolution time; (B) training completion and sign-off rates; (C) share of frauds found by proactive controls (analytics, IA) versus by accident – higher is better; (D) losses recovered.
Distractors: (E) The number of policies issued doesn't reflect real effectiveness (ICA-057).

FRD-092.q: A remote subsidiary posts the group's fastest profit growth; its director earns large bonuses and refuses internal audit visits. The group's appropriate response:
FRD-092.e: Incentive (bonus), opportunity (remote, light oversight) and avoidance behaviour together are strong red flags.
o: Treat as high risk; surprise audit, remote analytics, independent customer/vendor confirmations
FRD-092.x:
Basis: ACFE; VSA 240 appendix 1 (fraud risk factors).
Analysis: All three triangle sides converge: incentive (big profit-linked bonus), opportunity (remote, little oversight) and evasive behaviour (refusing IA) – a strong red flag. Response: treat as high risk; surprise audit; remote analytics (revenue, receivables, inventory, journals); independent confirmations with customers and vendors; defer bonus payment until verified; inform the audit committee.
Distractors: B, C and D increase risk or ignore the flag.

FRD-093.q: Transferring funds between bank accounts around period end so cash appears in two places (kiting) can conceal shortages.
FRD-093.e: True. An inter-bank transfer schedule helps detect it.
FRD-093.x:
Basis: ACFE – cash schemes (cheque kiting); VSA 500 (AUD-043).
Analysis: True. Kiting: transferring cash from account A to B around year-end, recording the increase in B but not yet the decrease in A (or exploiting float) → the same money appears twice, hiding a cash shortage. Detection: a bank transfer schedule around year-end, comparing book dates with bank debit/credit dates, obtaining next-period bank statements directly.

FRD-094.q: A tip alleges the CFO colludes with a supplier. Who should lead the investigation?
FRD-094.e: Independence is essential when the suspect is senior management.
o: The Audit Committee/Board, possibly with independent forensic experts; the CFO excluded
The chief accountant reporting to the CFO
FRD-094.x:
Basis: ACFE; IIA GIAS 2024 (independence, direct board reporting); Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (internal audit).
Analysis: The suspect is the CFO – senior management with authority over accounting and treasury → the audit committee/board must lead, possibly hiring independent forensic investigators; the CFO must be excluded from the investigation and its information, with access restricted if needed (FRD-066).
Distractors: B investigates himself; C – the chief accountant reports to the CFO and isn't independent; D – the vendor is a named party.

FRD-095.q: Of 10,000 payments, a round-amount test (divisible by VND 1 million) flags 1,200; the normal rate from industry experience is 5%. How many payments exceed the normal level?
FRD-095.e: Expected 10,000 × 5% = 500; excess 1,200 − 500 = 700 → prioritise round-sum items by preparer/vendor.
FRD-095.x:
Basis: ACFE – round-number testing; Nigrini.
Working: Expected = 10,000 × 5% = 500; excess = 1,200 − 500 = 700 payments.
Analysis: The actual 12% rate is 2.4× normal → round amounts often signal estimates, fabrication or costs lacking real invoices. Prioritise testing round-amount clusters by preparer, vendor, expense type and timing.
Check: 1,200 / 10,000 = 12% ✓.

FRD-096.q: A salesperson at a branch also collects cash; customers get 'handwritten receipts'. Controls to apply immediately:
FRD-096.e: Unnumbered handwritten receipts are a skimming opportunity.
o: System-numbered e-receipts/e-invoices, promote bank/QR payment to company accounts, confirm balances with customers
Let staff hold cash till month-end
FRD-096.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10; ACFE (skimming); Decree 123/2020/ND-CP (e-invoices and e-documents).
Analysis: A seller who also collects cash with handwritten, unnumbered receipts → opportunity for skimming (unrecorded collections) and lapping. Immediate controls: system-generated, sequentially numbered e-receipts/invoices; encourage bank transfer/QR payments to company accounts; daily deposits; independent customer balance confirmations (FRD-012).
Distractors: B, C and D keep or increase the opportunity.

FRD-097.q: Consider these statements on anti-fraud culture:
FRD-097.e: Documents without enforcement don't create culture.
o: Leaders must set an example and handle breaches consistently.
A written code of conduct alone is enough.
Rewarding good-faith whistleblowers can encourage reporting.
FRD-097.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P1.
Analysis: True – leaders modelling behaviour and consistent discipline underpin culture (ICA-086). False – a written code without enforcement creates no culture (ICA-057). True – communicating (anonymised) outcomes raises the perceived chance of detection, deterring fraud (FRD-061). True – rewarding good-faith reporters encourages reporting.
Note: Rewards should be designed to avoid bad-faith reports.

FRD-098.q: Internal audit finds a haulier paid 15% above 3 competitive quotes; the proposer is the warehouse head whose brother works there. On purchases of VND 4,000 million, what is the estimated loss (assuming competitive prices are the benchmark)?
FRD-098.e: Benchmark = 4,000/1.15 ≈ 3,478; difference ≈ 522 million VND (not 15% × 4,000 = 600, since 15% is on the benchmark).
FRD-098.x:
Basis: ACFE – loss measurement (corruption, conflicts of interest).
Working: Benchmark (competitive) price = 4,000 / 1.15 ≈ 3,478.3 million; loss = 4,000 − 3,478.3 ≈ 521.7 ≈ VND 522 million.
Analysis: 15% is a markup over the benchmark, so divide by 1.15 rather than apply 15% to the amount paid. The real loss also depends on whether service quality was equivalent. With the conflict of interest (the warehouse head's brother works at the vendor) → investigate possible kickbacks.
Check: 3,478.3 × 1.15 ≈ 4,000 ✓.

FRD-099.q: In the ACFE Fraud Tree, 'billing schemes' fall under:
FRD-099.e: They include shell vendors, false/inflated invoices from real vendors and personal purchases with company funds.
FRD-099.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Tree.
Analysis: Billing schemes sit under asset misappropriation → cash → fraudulent disbursements, covering: shell companies (FRD-013); false, inflated or duplicate invoices from real non-accomplice vendors; personal purchases with company funds. Other disbursement schemes: payroll, expense reimbursement, cheque tampering, register disbursements.
Distractors: B – corruption is a separate branch (though pass-throughs may involve conflicts); C and D misclassify.

FRD-100.q: Select ALL items a fraud investigation report should contain:
FRD-100.e: Guilt is for the judicial authorities; internal reports state facts and evidence only.
o: A conclusion on an individual's criminal guilt
FRD-100.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual (report writing); Criminal Procedure Code 2015 (presumption of innocence – Art. 13).
Analysis: An investigation report should include: (A) scope, methods and evidence sources; (B) verified facts kept separate from speculation; (C) quantified loss and its basis (FRD-098); (D) control deficiencies and remediation recommendations (FRD-070). Write objectively, without conclusions on motive or guilt.
Distractors: (E) Criminal guilt is for the judicial authorities; a suspect is presumed innocent until a final judgment.
